messages.subject: mlik to calculate Bayes factor
parts:
Hi, 
Could anyone confirm my understanding of the "mlik" output? Or point out any document that provides some detailed information about the output list given by summary(result)? 
It seems that result$mlik has two rows: 

"log marginal-likelihood (integration)"

 "log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian)

1) could you tell what integration and Gaussian stands for? different approximation methods? I noticed that the difference is tiny in my case. If I want to calculate the Bayes factor, does this matter? 

2) Is the marginal likelihood given in result$mlik on the log scale? say I want to compare two models, result1 and result0, does this mean that log(BF10)= result1$mlik["log marginal-likelihood (integration)",1] - result0$mlik["log marginal-likelihood (integration)",1] 

Many thanks, 

Joyce

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mlik to calculate Bayes factor
parts:
Yes it's on the log scale.

Gaussian refers to what you get assuming the posterior for the hyperparametrs are jointly Gaussian.  Integration is using the integration points to integrate the posterior for theta. Default integration method correct for skewness in the post for theta, and should be more accurate than the Gaussian one. 

These details will appear I the INLA tutorial that is in writing...  Thanks for asking these good questions!
(and in a paper that Thiago is writing at the moment....)

messages.author: 3eab71733027a24a
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] mlik to calculate Bayes factor
parts:
its discussed in the JRSSB 2009 paper.

and the approximation of \pi(\theta| y) we use is from the 'new
features' paper, and by integrating this approximation this is what
gives the marginal likelihood estimate ``integration''

> inla(y~1,data=data.frame(y=0))$mlik
[,1]
log marginal-likelihood (integration) -0.001348612533
log marginal-likelihood (Gaussian) -0.081220457277


whereas the 'Gaussian' is just treating \pi(\theta | y) as Gaussian,
which is classical ``estimating marginal likelihood using laplace
approximation'' approach.
